titleStmt.title: Dopamine Cells Respond to Predicted Events during Classical Conditioning: Evidence for Eligibility Traces in the Reward-Learning Network
titleStmt.author: Wei‐Xing Pan
Robert Schmidt
Jeffery R. Wickens
Brian I. Hyland

bibl.title: Dopamine Cells Respond to Predicted Events during Classical Conditioning: Evidence for Eligibility Traces in the Reward-Learning Network

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how the dopamine response moves from reward to predictive cue during learning, and whether the temporal difference algorithm can produce that time course
span.quote: Behavioral conditioning of cue-reward pairing results in a shift of midbrain dopamine (DA) cell activity from responding to the reward to responding to the predictive cue. However, the precise time course and mechanism underlying this shift remain unclear.

span.label: whether dopamine cells show the stepwise latency migration that published TD models predict, and if not, which parameter settings would reproduce what they do show
span.quote: In this study, we first investigated in conscious rats whether DA cells conform to these specific patterns of prediction error signaling by recording from single neurons while animals first learned the association between cues and rewards. The results were not consistent with previous model predictions. We then performed a systematic exploration of the parameter space of the TD algorithm to determine whether it can encompass the activity patterns displayed by the DA cells.

span.label: shows cue and reward responses coexist rather than trading off, then finds the pattern is reproduced only by long eligibility traces and a low learning rate - turning physiology into a constraint on the algorithm's parameters
span.quote: By exploring the TD parameter space, we demonstrate that the persistent reward responses of DA cells during conditioning are only accurately replicated by a TD model with long-lasting eligibility traces (nonzero values for the parameter λ) and low learning rate (α).

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: By exploring the TD parameter space, we demonstrate that the persistent reward responses of DA cells during conditioning are only accurately replicated by a TD model with long-lasting eligibility traces (nonzero values for the parameter λ) and low learning rate (α).

span.label: dopamine reward-prediction-error signalling during classical conditioning
span.quote: Behavioral conditioning of cue-reward pairing results in a shift of midbrain dopamine (DA) cell activity from responding to the reward to responding to the predictive cue.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Here, we report a combined single-unit recording and temporal difference (TD) modeling approach to this question.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A long-lasting eligibility trace keeps the weights of an earlier sensory signal open to modification for many time steps, so the reward-driven prediction error can be assigned back to the cue in one step instead of migrating one time step per trial
span.quote: In TD(λ), vector weights representing a sensory signal remain eligible for modification by prediction error signals for a variable number of time steps after the signal has occurred.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A very low learning rate combined with a high eligibility-trace decay makes each trial change the weights only slightly, so responses to the cue and to the predicted reward coexist for a prolonged period before the reward response is suppressed
span.quote: Thus, very low α in combination with high λ generates a prolonged period over which both cue and reward responses occur, as seen in the DA cell data.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Sustained firing in reverberating circuits, or biochemical processes at the synapse, could hold the seconds-long eligibility trace the model requires
span.quote: Potential mechanisms include sustained firing in reverberating circuits and biochemical mechanisms acting at the synaptic level ( Houk et al., 1995 ).

span.label: an eligibility trace keeps earlier time steps modifiable, so a cue several steps back can be updated in one trial instead of waiting for the error to migrate
span.quote: The eligibility trace enables weights associated with previous time steps to be altered by prediction error at time step t and was calculated recursively ( Sutton, 1988 ) by the following: e l ( t + 1) = λ e l ( t ) + x l ( t ) , where λ is the eligibility trace decay parameter.

span.label: with a low learning rate each trial moves the weights only slightly, which is what lets cue and reward responses coexist for hundreds of trials
span.quote: Otherwise, the value for α, given a suitable setting for λ, determined the number of trials needed for growth of the cue response and for abolition of the reward response and therefore the number of trials over which these responses coexisted.

span.label: under TD(0) the error must arrive one step earlier per trial, so reaching a cue k steps back takes at least k trials
span.quote: A physiological interpretation of TD(0) is that the system can only hold a memory of an event from one moment to the next. Our findings suggest that this limitation cannot apply to learning in the brain reward pathways.

span.label: candidate substrates for a seconds-long trace are reverberating circuits and synaptic biochemistry
span.quote: The existence of eligibility traces lasting several seconds in neural circuits is open to experimental verification. Potential mechanisms include sustained firing in reverberating circuits and biochemical mechanisms acting at the synaptic level

span.label: long traces with slow learning is the combination machine learning already found to give early but stable learning, which may be why biology uses it
span.quote: Thus, combining prolonged eligibility for change with low rates for learning rate offers considerable practical advantages that may have provided significant selective pressure for the coevolution of equivalent parameter settings in the brain.

span.label: The fitted parameter values are not claimed to be fixed neural constants, since a different model structure could yield different best-fitting values.
span.note: what this limits: the fitted parameter values: OUR RESULTS SHOULD NOT BE UNDERSTOOD AS PROVIDING EXPLICIT FIXED VALUES FOR NEURAL TD LEARNING PARAMETERS, BECAUSE THE SPECIFIC VALUES ... MAY BE DIFFERENT IF DETAILS OF THE MODEL STRUCTURE WERE CHANGED
span.quote: It is important to note that our results should not be understood as providing explicit fixed values for neural TD learning parameters, because the specific values that produce the best fit to the data may be different if details of the model structure were changed.

span.label: The stimulus representation assumed by the model (serial compound) is not known to be how the brain represents stimuli for reward learning.
span.note: what this limits: the timing predictions in particular: IT IS NOT KNOWN HOW SENSORY STIMULI ARE REPRESENTED IN THE BRAIN FOR REWARD LEARNING
span.quote: For instance, it is not known how sensory stimuli are represented in the brain for reward learning.

span.label: the paper refuses the strong reading of its own result: these are not fixed values for neural parameters, because a different model structure would shift them
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 0 - the values are a property of this model structure
span.quote: It is important to note that our results should not be understood as providing explicit fixed values for neural TD learning parameters, because the specific values that produce the best fit to the data may be different if details of the model structure were changed. For instance, it is not known how sensory stimuli are represented in the brain for reward learning. We followed many previous studies in using a serial compound representation of conditioned stimuli. Alternative representations can be envisaged (Suri and Schultz, 1998 , 1999 ), which might lead to different specific parameter values.

span.label: how the brain represents stimuli in time is unknown; the serial compound representation is a convention inherited from earlier models
span.note: what this limits: the same scope as item 1, with the convention named: WE FOLLOWED MANY PREVIOUS STUDIES IN USING A SERIAL COMPOUND REPRESENTATION OF CONDITIONED STIMULI
span.quote: For instance, it is not known how sensory stimuli are represented in the brain for reward learning. We followed many previous studies in using a serial compound representation of conditioned stimuli.

span.label: the animals had already had hundreds of solenoid-reward pairings before recording, so the click was not a neutral event at the start of conditioning
span.note: what this limits: any reading of the click as a neutral cue: ANIMALS WERE THEREFORE EXPOSED TO HUNDREDS OF SOLENOID-REWARD PAIRINGS BY THE TIME THE RECORDINGS WERE MADE
span.quote: We ran the random-reward condition while searching for cells in case it activated otherwise-quiescent neurons. Animals were therefore exposed to hundreds of solenoid-reward pairings by the time the recordings were made.

span.label: the negative prediction error signal is small and hard to measure against an already low baseline rate
span.note: what this limits: the negative prediction-error signal: THE AMPLITUDE OF INHIBITIONS WAS SMALL, CONSISTENT WITH THE FACT THAT INHIBITORY RESPONSES CAN BE DIFFICULT TO DETECT AND QUANTIFY IN NEURONS THAT ALREADY HAVE A LOW BASELINE RATE
span.quote: The amplitude of inhibitions was small, consistent with the fact that inhibitory responses can be difficult to detect and quantify in neurons that already have a low baseline rate of activity, as noted previously in primate studies

span.label: 21 of 45 electrophysiologically plausible cells failed the pharmacological test and were discarded
span.note: what this limits: what a 'dopamine neuron' means here, and in every study that skips the drug test: FROM 45 NEURONS THAT WERE POSSIBLY DOPAMINERGIC ON ELECTROPHYSIOLOGICAL CRITERIA, 24 ... WERE CONFIRMED DA NEURONS BASED ON HAVING A CLEAR INHIBITORY RESPONSE TO DOPAMINE AGONIST DRUGS
span.quote: From 45 neurons that were possibly dopaminergic on electrophysiological criteria, 24 recorded from 11 rats were confirmed DA neurons based on having a clear inhibitory response to dopamine agonist drugs

span.label: The temporal difference algorithm and its prediction-error signal, taken from machine learning, are used as the model of midbrain dopamine cell activity.
span.quote: Furthermore, several features of DA cell activity match properties of the prediction error signal of the temporal difference (TD) algorithm for machine learning, leading to the hypothesis that DA cell activity may be providing a teaching signal within a neural analog of a TD learning system in the brain

span.label: the temporal difference algorithm, imported as a candidate account of what dopamine cells compute
span.quote: In the temporal difference algorithm, an estimate of the expected reward at a particular time step t is derived from the difference between the prediction of all future rewards at that time step, P ( t ), and the prediction of all future rewards that was generated at the previous time step, P ( t - 1) ( Sutton, 1988 ). The difference between these successive predictions represents reward expected to occur at time t . It is this component of the algorithm, which involves calculating a difference between two successive time steps, that gives rise to the term temporal difference.

span.label: the century-old requirement that some trace of the cue survive until the reward arrives, here identified with the eligibility trace
span.quote: The concept that for delayed associative conditioning to occur there must be some memory or trace of the antecedent signal at the time of a subsequent reward is as old as the study of classical conditioning itself

span.label: the known trade-off that high lambda with low alpha buys stable early learning, used here as an adaptive argument
span.quote: A low learning rate may be considered a disadvantage. However, previous studies in machine learning have found that when λ is set high to enable learning to begin early in training, low values of α improve the stability of learning

span.label: electrode track positions confirmed histologically after the experiments were completed
span.note: eliminates: attributing the responses to dopamine cells that were not where the recordings were thought to be - the confirmation comes after, from the tissue, not from the coordinates
span.quote: The position of the electrode tracks was confirmed after completion of the experiments.

span.label: presumed DA cells are a doubly filtered category: rate below 10 Hz and spike at least 1 ms, THEN more than 50% inhibition by a dopamine agonist. Cell identity is pharmacological here, not genetic or anatomical
span.quote: From this group, only cells that were also profoundly (>50%) inhibited by the dopamine agonist apomorphine (750 μg/kg, i.p.) or the D 2 receptor-selective agonist quinpirole (400 μg/kg, s.c.) were accepted as presumed DA cells

span.label: TD(0), TD(1) and TD(lambda) are three different models, not one - the value of lambda changes which weights an error can touch, and the published DA models were TD(0)
span.quote: If λ = 1, all weights are affected equally [TD(1) model]. If λ = 0, only weights associated with the immediate previous state are affected [TD(0) model]. The effect when 0 < λ < 1 is to exponentially bias weight change so that vectors representing the most recent events are affected the most by the prediction error signal [TD(λ) model].

span.label: prediction error here is the scalar difference between actual reward and the temporal difference of successive predictions, with the NEGATIVE side deliberately clipped to match dopamine cells' floor
span.quote: To model this, we applied a limit to the amplitude of the negative prediction error such that negative and positive prediction errors were scaled in a similar way to the dynamic range of dopamine cell activity. In preliminary runs of the model, we found that the largest positive prediction error values approached 1, which can be equated to the maximum firing rate (100 Hz) in DA cells. The maximum negative prediction error was therefore limited to -0.05.

span.label: early and late training are defined by block count - 6 or fewer against 10 or more - and the paper's central result holds only early
span.quote: It is notable that unlike the persistent responses seen in DA cells recorded early in training, cells recorded after many sessions of cue-reward pairing were unresponsive to predictable reward delivery

span.label: the recorded population pools substantia nigra pars compacta, ventral tegmental area and supramammillary nucleus, justified by a null on regional differences
span.quote: There was no regional difference in response patterns, so all cells from all regions were pooled for analysis.

span.label: claim_type: mechanism
span.note: a second reading reaching the same value. Recorded: mechanism — a second reading reaching the same value from a different sentence. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: These physiological constraints for TD parameters suggest that eligibility traces and low per-trial rates of plastic modification may be essential features of neural circuits for reward learning in the brain. Such properties enable rapid but stable initiation of learning when the number of stimulus-reward pairings is limited, conferring significant adaptive advantages in real-world environments.

span.label: method: extracellular single-unit recording from pharmacologically identified midbrain dopamine cells during first acquisition, paired with a systematic sweep of the TD algorithm's parameter space
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: electrophysiology — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: In this study, we first investigated in conscious rats whether DA cells conform to these specific patterns of prediction error signaling by recording from single neurons while animals first learned the association between cues and rewards. The results were not consistent with previous model predictions. We then performed a systematic exploration of the parameter space of the TD algorithm to determine whether it can encompass the activity patterns displayed by the DA cells.

span.label: phenomenon: the shift of dopamine cell firing from unexpected reward to the cue that predicts it
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: dopamine reward-prediction-error signalling during classical conditioning — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Behavioral conditioning of cue-reward pairing results in a shift of midbrain dopamine (DA) cell activity from responding to the reward to responding to the predictive cue. However, the precise time course and mechanism underlying this shift remain unclear.

span.label: builds-on → Montague et al. (1996) temporal-difference model of dopamine activity
span.quote: The TD algorithm we used to model DA cell activity was based on that described by Montague et al. ( 1996 ).

span.label: contradicts → previous TD models predicting a gradual stepwise latency shift (Montague et al., 1996; Schultz et al., 1997)
span.note: differs in: the time course of the latency shift: previous TD models PREDICT A GRADUAL STEPWISE SHIFT IN LATENCY WITH RESPONSES TO REWARDS LOST BEFORE RESPONSES DEVELOP TO THE CONDITIONED CUE
span.quote: This contrasts with previous TD models that predict a gradual stepwise shift in latency with responses to rewards lost before responses develop to the conditioned cue.

span.label: extends → Miller et al., 1981; Kosobud et al., 1994; Kiyatkin and Rebec, 2001; Hyland et al., 2002 (rat DA cell responses to reward-predicting cues)
span.quote: These results extend previous findings from rats that DA cells respond to sensory cues predicting reward ( Miller et al., 1981 ; Kosobud et al., 1994 ; Kiyatkin and Rebec, 2001 ; Hyland et al., 2002 ) and show for the first time that these are contingent on cue-reward association and arise during acquisition of classically conditioned behavior.

span.label: contradicts → the stepwise latency migration predicted by TD(0) models of dopamine activity
span.note: differs in: the latency profile of the new response: NEW CONDITIONED RESPONSES MADE THEIR FIRST APPEARANCE AT A CONSTANT, SHORT LATENCY AFTER PREDICTIVE CUES, and DEVELOPED RAPIDLY, WITHIN A FEW TRIALS - not the gradual migration the models expect
span.quote: Importantly, in contrast to previous model expectations, we found that new conditioned responses made their first appearance at a constant, short latency after predictive cues in conditioning with either a single ( Fig. 2 A ) or double ( Fig. 2 B ) cue. These new responses developed rapidly, within a few trials, as can be seen in the dot raster displays of trial-by-trial cell activity. Thus, in these experiments, we found no evidence for a gradual shift in latency of the responses.

span.label: contradicts → the prediction that a redundant intermediate cue draws no response
span.quote: Similarly, we found that in all cells conditioned with two cues presented in sequence there was a clear response to the second cue, which persisted throughout the experiment ( Fig. 2 B ). An additional cell tested with a tone-light cue sequence (data not shown) also responded to both cues.

span.label: contradicts → the prediction that reward responses vanish before cue responses appear
span.quote: Finally, we found that responses to reward remained long after the new responses to the predictive cues had developed. This was true both for cells recorded with a single cue ( Fig. 2 A ) and in the two-cue paradigm ( Fig. 2 B ) and was seen in all cells recorded in early training.

span.label: reconciles → the temporal difference framework with the recorded time course, by relocating the disagreement to parameter choice
span.note: differs in: the model's free parameters: THESE APPARENT DISPARITIES BETWEEN TD MODEL PREDICTION ERRORS AND DA CELL ACTIVITY ARE ATTRIBUTABLE TO THE PARTICULAR CHOICE OF PARAMETERS USED IN THE MODEL - the settings for ALPHA and LAMBDA, not the framework
span.quote: However, when we investigated the effects of different settings for the parameters α and λ of the TD algorithm, we found that these apparent disparities between TD model prediction errors and DA cell activity are attributable to the particular choice of parameters used in the model. Thus, instead of posing a problem for TD models, the present results show that classical TD mechanisms can account for a wider range of observed DA cell behaviors than previously envisaged.

span.label: critiques → published primate datasets, which on re-inspection never supported gradual migration either
span.note: differs in: gradual migration against simultaneous responding, and the stage of learning: the existing primate data PROVIDES NO SUPPORT FOR THE GRADUAL MIGRATION OF A RESPONSE DURING LEARNING AND SUGGESTS THAT DA CELLS SHOW SIMULTANEOUS RESPONDING TO BOTH CUE AND REWARD, AT LEAST EARLY IN LEARNING
span.quote: Inspection of existing data sets from primates also provides no support for the gradual migration of a response during learning ( Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1994 ; Hollerman and Schultz, 1998 ; Waelti et al., 2001 ; Takikawa et al., 2004 ) and suggests that DA cells show simultaneous responding to both cue and reward, at least early in learning

span.label: confirms → earlier reports that reward responses are diminished in highly trained animals
span.quote: These data indicate that the development of conditioned responses to cues does not directly lead to abolishment of responses to rewards. Rather, responses to predicted rewards are only completely lost after a period of training that extends beyond that required to first establish conditioned responses to predictive cues.

span.label: extends → rat studies showing dopamine responses to reward-predicting cues, by showing they arise during acquisition
span.quote: These results extend previous findings from rats that DA cells respond to sensory cues predicting reward ( Miller et al., 1981 ; Kosobud et al., 1994 ; Kiyatkin and Rebec, 2001 ; Hyland et al., 2002 ) and show for the first time that these are contingent on cue-reward association and arise during acquisition of classically conditioned behavior.

span.label: prediction error —operationalised-as→ DA cells
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the identification is asymmetric by construction: firing can rise to 100 Hz but only fall to zero from a 5 Hz baseline
span.quote: The baseline spiking activity of DA cells (∼5 Hz) can be equated to a state of 0 prediction error ( Schultz et al., 1997 ). Spike activity can only be suppressed from this baseline down to 0 Hz. On the other hand, DA cells can be transiently excited to instantaneous rates of up to 100 Hz ( Hyland et al., 2002 ). They are therefore very asymmetrical in the range of positive and negative prediction error signal amplitudes they can generate.

span.label: eligibility trace —distinct-from→ learning rate
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — CRITERION: lambda decides WHETHER stepwise migration happens at all, alpha decides HOW LONG cue and reward responses overlap
span.quote: Otherwise, the value for α, given a suitable setting for λ, determined the number of trials needed for growth of the cue response and for abolition of the reward response and therefore the number of trials over which these responses coexisted.

span.label: TD(0) —is-a→ temporal difference
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: If λ = 1, all weights are affected equally [TD(1) model]. If λ = 0, only weights associated with the immediate previous state are affected [TD(0) model]. The effect when 0 < λ < 1 is to exponentially bias weight change so that vectors representing the most recent events are affected the most by the prediction error signal [TD(λ) model].

span.label: TD(1) —is-a→ temporal difference
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: If λ = 1, all weights are affected equally [TD(1) model]. If λ = 0, only weights associated with the immediate previous state are affected [TD(0) model]. The effect when 0 < λ < 1 is to exponentially bias weight change so that vectors representing the most recent events are affected the most by the prediction error signal [TD(λ) model].

span.label: TD(0) —operationalised-as→ eligibility trace
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — TD(0) IS the lambda = 0 case, so a claim about TD(0) is a claim about one setting and not about the framework
span.quote: If λ = 1, all weights are affected equally [TD(1) model]. If λ = 0, only weights associated with the immediate previous state are affected [TD(0) model]. The effect when 0 < λ < 1 is to exponentially bias weight change so that vectors representing the most recent events are affected the most by the prediction error signal [TD(λ) model].

span.label: apomorphine —operationalised-as→ DA cells
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — direction is test-to-category: more than 50% inhibition by the agonist is what makes a recorded cell count as dopaminergic
span.quote: From this group, only cells that were also profoundly (>50%) inhibited by the dopamine agonist apomorphine (750 μg/kg, i.p.) or the D 2 receptor-selective agonist quinpirole (400 μg/kg, s.c.) were accepted as presumed DA cells

span.label: substantia nigra pars compacta —contrasted-with→ ventral tegmental area
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.5 — the record marks this weak — a contrast the paper DECLINES to draw, on the strength of a null - the two regions are pooled for every analysis
span.quote: There was no regional difference in response patterns, so all cells from all regions were pooled for analysis.

span.label: eligibility trace —causes→ conditioned
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — the trace is what lets a cue and a later reward be associated at all; the requirement predates the algorithm by eighty years
span.quote: The concept that for delayed associative conditioning to occur there must be some memory or trace of the antecedent signal at the time of a subsequent reward is as old as the study of classical conditioning itself

span.label: serial compound —operationalised-as→ state vector
span.note: strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Stimuli were represented in the state vectors as a complete serial compound stimulus. In this kind of representation, if a stimulus has occurred, then one component of the vector is “1,” and all others are “0.” Which of the components is set at 1 at any one time depends on the number of time steps that have passed since stimulus occurrence. Thus, component q of the state vector is 1 if the stimulus presentation was exactly q - 1 time steps ago and 0 otherwise

span.label: omission —operationalised-as→ prediction error
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — the negative side of the signal is measured by withholding what was predicted
span.quote: Quantitative analysis of the period 200 ms after the expected time of the second cue compared with baseline in seven cells tested with cue 2 omission in the two-cue paradigm yielded an average modulation index at the time of the expected cue of -0.12 ± 0.17 (mean ± SD; where 0 = normalized baseline), which represented a nonsignificant difference from baseline firing rate. However, a significant reduction in firing rate was observed when expected rewards were omitted (average modulation index, -0.21 ± 0.20; p < 0.01; paired t test; n = 11).

span.label: modulation index —operationalised-as→ DA cells
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.7 — normalisation to a pre-cue baseline is what makes cells with different firing rates poolable
span.quote: To enable comparison of changes in firing rate induced by task events under different conditions across different cells, we normalized histogram firing rates by calculating a modulation index

span.label: supramammillary nucleus —part-of→ DA cells
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak — included in the recorded population; not conventionally a dopaminergic cell group, and the pooling is justified only by the regional null
span.quote: This group had an average firing rate of 5.7 ± 3.5 Hz (mean ± SD), action potential duration of 1.5 ± 1.3 ms, and were located in the midbrain dopamine cell fields ( Fig. 1 B ) including both medial A9 (substantia nigra pars compacta) and lateral A10 (ventral tegmental area and supramammillary nucleus).

span.label: t-test
span.quote: However, a significant reduction in firing rate was observed when expected rewards were omitted (average modulation index, -0.21 ± 0.20; p < 0.01; paired t test; n = 11).

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: This group had an average firing rate of 5.7 ± 3.5 Hz (mean ± SD), action potential duration of 1.5 ± 1.3 ms

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: Population histograms below the rasters were calculated by averaging 50 ms bin counts across all individual histograms ( n = 6, 8, and 3, respectively) and converting to instantaneous frequency. Error bars represent SEM.

span.label: standard deviation threshold criterion
span.quote: Latency was measured from the left edge of the first bin of a peak or trough after an event that was ≥2 SDs of the mean baseline firing rate (calculated from the 2 s before the first event).

span.label: histogram
span.quote: Changes in firing rate associated with task events were examined by constructing trial-by-trial dot raster displays and averaged peri-event time histograms.

span.label: paired t test
span.quote: Quantitative analysis of the period 200 ms after the expected time of the second cue compared with baseline in seven cells tested with cue 2 omission in the two-cue paradigm yielded an average modulation index at the time of the expected cue of -0.12 ± 0.17 (mean ± SD; where 0 = normalized baseline), which represented a nonsignificant difference from baseline firing rate. However, a significant reduction in firing rate was observed when expected rewards were omitted (average modulation index, -0.21 ± 0.20; p < 0.01; paired t test; n = 11).

span.label: modulation index
span.quote: To enable comparison of changes in firing rate induced by task events under different conditions across different cells, we normalized histogram firing rates by calculating a modulation index

span.label: SD
span.quote: This group had an average firing rate of 5.7 ± 3.5 Hz (mean ± SD), action potential duration of 1.5 ± 1.3 ms, and were located in the midbrain dopamine cell fields ( Fig. 1 B ) including both medial A9 (substantia nigra pars compacta) and lateral A10 (ventral tegmental area and supramammillary nucleus).

span.label: Dopamine cells went on responding to the reward long after they had developed responses to the predictive cue, contradicting the prediction that the reward response dies before the cue response appears.
span.quote: Finally, we found that responses to reward remained long after the new responses to the predictive cues had developed.

span.label: New conditioned responses appeared straight away at their final short latency after the cue, with no gradual backward drift of latency from reward to cue.
span.quote: Importantly, in contrast to previous model expectations, we found that new conditioned responses made their first appearance at a constant, short latency after predictive cues in conditioning with either a single ( Fig. 2 A ) or double ( Fig. 2 B ) cue.

span.label: Every cell trained with two cues in sequence responded clearly to the second, seemingly redundant cue, and that response persisted for the whole experiment.
span.quote: Similarly, we found that in all cells conditioned with two cues presented in sequence there was a clear response to the second cue, which persisted throughout the experiment ( Fig. 2 B ).

span.label: Cells recorded after many sessions of cue-reward pairing no longer responded to a predictable reward, unlike the cells recorded early in training.
span.quote: It is notable that unlike the persistent responses seen in DA cells recorded early in training, cells recorded after many sessions of cue-reward pairing were unresponsive to predictable reward delivery ( Fig. 3 B , middle).

span.label: Acquiring a cue response and losing the reward response run on different time courses rather than being two sides of one shift.
span.quote: Together, these data suggest that there are different time courses for acquisition of new conditioned responses to cues and the loss of responses to the rewards predicted by those cues.

span.label: Omitting an expected reward produced a significant drop in firing rate, whereas omitting the expected second cue did not differ significantly from baseline.
span.quote: However, a significant reduction in firing rate was observed when expected rewards were omitted (average modulation index, -0.21 ± 0.20; p < 0.01; paired t test; n = 11).

span.label: Leaving out the second cue restored the dopamine response to the reward up to the level seen when reward was delivered at random, both early and late in training.
span.quote: We also observed that compared with trials in which reward was preceded by two cues, omission of the second cue ( Fig. 3 , right) restored responses to the solenoid to levels seen with random reward ( Fig. 3 , left).

span.label: Setting the eligibility-trace decay to 0.9 and the learning rate to 0.005 made the TD model reproduce the recorded dopamine pattern, including a time-locked response to the intermediate cue and coexisting cue and reward responses.
span.quote: With these values, the prediction error signal output reproduced key elements of the pattern seen during learning in our DA cell recording experiments ( Fig. 4 D ).

span.label: A high eligibility-trace decay parameter was the one setting that let the model learn cue significance without stepwise trial-by-trial migration of the response from reward to cue.
span.quote: Examination of three-dimensional (3-D) plots of model performance over a range of parameter settings ( Fig. 5 ) showed that high values of λ were the critical factor that enabled the model to learn about the significance of cues without gradual trial-by-trial stepwise migration of responses from rewards to cues.

span.label: Once the eligibility-trace decay fell below about 0.6, stepwise migration of the prediction error reappeared no matter what learning rate was used.
span.quote: As λ was reduced below a threshold level (∼0.6 for the number of time steps modeled here), step-wise migration of prediction error signals appeared for all values of α.

span.label: conditioned responses appeared at their final short latency within a few trials, with no gradual migration
span.quote: Importantly, in contrast to previous model expectations, we found that new conditioned responses made their first appearance at a constant, short latency after predictive cues in conditioning with either a single ( Fig. 2 A ) or double ( Fig. 2 B ) cue. These new responses developed rapidly, within a few trials, as can be seen in the dot raster displays of trial-by-trial cell activity. Thus, in these experiments, we found no evidence for a gradual shift in latency of the responses.

span.label: the redundant intermediate cue drew a clear response in every two-cue cell, which persisted
span.quote: Similarly, we found that in all cells conditioned with two cues presented in sequence there was a clear response to the second cue, which persisted throughout the experiment ( Fig. 2 B ). An additional cell tested with a tone-light cue sequence (data not shown) also responded to both cues.

span.label: responses to predicted reward persisted after cue responses had developed, in every cell recorded early in training
span.quote: Finally, we found that responses to reward remained long after the new responses to the predictive cues had developed. This was true both for cells recorded with a single cue ( Fig. 2 A ) and in the two-cue paradigm ( Fig. 2 B ) and was seen in all cells recorded in early training.

span.label: after ten or more blocks the reward response was gone, so the two changes have different time courses
span.quote: These data indicate that the development of conditioned responses to cues does not directly lead to abolishment of responses to rewards. Rather, responses to predicted rewards are only completely lost after a period of training that extends beyond that required to first establish conditioned responses to predictive cues.

span.label: those late-training cells still responded to reward when it arrived uncued, so the loss is prediction-specific and not fatigue
span.quote: These cells were still capable of responding to the reward, as demonstrated by robust responses to solenoid activation when delivered without any cues ( Fig. 3 , left) or on trials in which the second cue was unexpectedly omitted

span.label: omitting the second cue restored the reward response to its uncued level, so the redundant cue was doing predictive work
span.quote: We also observed that compared with trials in which reward was preceded by two cues, omission of the second cue ( Fig. 3 , right) restored responses to the solenoid to levels seen with random reward ( Fig. 3 , left). This was the case both early and late in training. Thus, learning about the intermediate cue was not blocked by the presence of the preceding one, in the sense that the presence or absence of the second cue was taken into account in determining cell responses to the reward.

span.label: TD with eligibility zero and a fast learning rate reproduced the published pattern, with no second-cue response and no overlap
span.quote: Figure 4 B shows model prediction error output over learning trials for λ = 0 and α = 0.05. These settings produce a pattern of prediction error output similar to that reported previously ( Montague et al., 1996 ; Schultz et al., 1997 ). In particular, there is no clear time-locked response to the second cue, and the response to the first cue develops only after a gradual shift in response latency from the time of the reward to the time of the first cue. During this time, there is no response time-locked to either the first cue or the reward, so that there is no overlap in time between cue and reward responses.

span.label: TD with lambda 0.9 and alpha 0.005 reproduced the recorded pattern, including the coexistence and the intermediate cue response
span.quote: In contrast, Figure 4 C shows the result for λ = 0.9, with α = 0.005. span.label: temporal difference
span.quote: In the temporal difference algorithm, an estimate of the expected reward at a particular time step t is derived from the difference between the prediction of all future rewards at that time step, P ( t ), and the prediction of all future rewards that was generated at the previous time step, P ( t - 1) ( Sutton, 1988 ). The difference between these successive predictions represents reward expected to occur at time t . It is this component of the algorithm, which involves calculating a difference between two successive time steps, that gives rise to the term temporal difference.

span.label: serial compound
span.quote: Stimuli were represented in the state vectors as a complete serial compound stimulus. In this kind of representation, if a stimulus has occurred, then one component of the vector is “1,” and all others are “0.” Which of the components is set at 1 at any one time depends on the number of time steps that have passed since stimulus occurrence. Thus, component q of the state vector is 1 if the stimulus presentation was exactly q - 1 time steps ago and 0 otherwise

span.label: 74 ms and 53 ms — latency of the new conditioned excitations and inhibitions
span.quote: Dopamine cells displayed rapid response plasticity during classical conditioning of cue-reward associations. DA cells responded to random reward, and then new responses to tone cues developed rapidly when these were paired with reward. Typical features of the development of conditioned responses during learning are illustrated in Figure 2 . New short-latency responses (excitations, 74 ± 33 ms; inhibitions, 53 ± 9 ms) began within the first block of training. This cellular conditioning occurred in most cells tested (8 of 11) and developed over a similar time course to the development of conditioned behavior (licking responses to the cues).
